newsitem.title: USA: Bonnie and Clyde might be buried together.
newsitem.headline: Bonnie and Clyde might be buried together.

text.p: Legendary outlaws Bonnie Parker and Clyde Barrow wanted to be buried together once their lives of crime came to an end. Now, almost 63 years after their bloody deaths, that might just happen.

Marie Barrow, Clyde's sister, plans to sell several of her infamous brother's personal belongings at an auction in San Francisco this month and says she would like to use some of the money raised to bury him with Parker.
"That was their death wish, especially hers. They wanted to be buried together," Barrow told Reuters on Tuesday. "That's what I hope to do, but I'll need to check it with her family."

Known as Bonnie and Clyde, the two young lovers, joined by other gang members, went on a 2-1/2 year spree of murders and bank robberies across the Southwest and Midwest before being killed in a police ambush near Gibsland, Louisiana, in May 1934.
The gang killed at least 12 law enforcement officers during their reign of terror, but their memory has been romanticized by a string of books and movies.

The film "Bonnie and Clyde," starring Warren Beatty and Faye Dunaway and directed by Arthur Penn, won two Oscars in 1967. It featured a slow-motion depiction of their death that stirred controversy because of its violence.
Parker's mother refused to grant her daughter's wish that she be buried with Barrow, and the two were buried in separate Dallas cemeteries.
Among the items Marie Barrow will put on the auction block on April 14 are her brother's pocket watch, a rifle he used when he was a boy, pictures of Bonnie and Clyde together, a belt and a necklace.

The bullet-riddled shirt that Barrow was wearing when he died is also to go on the block. Marie Barrow sold it last year to a Dallas collector and The Dallas Morning News said it had been valued by the San Francisco auction house at between $35,000 and $45,000.
It said the rest of Barrow's belongings about to go on sale are valued at between $21,000 to $31,000, but they could fetch much more.
Marie Barrow said her mother had kept Clyde's belongings in a cedar chest, refusing to sell them. "But I am getting old and I need the money," she said.
